item.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
item.description:
Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen further into a category 2 hurricane before approaching the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño this year, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. In fact, the first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

FBI seizes Chinese hacking tools used for cyberattacks on critical U.S. infrastructure
item.description:
The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and is believed responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power industry, academia and critical infrastructure.

The seizure of the tools, announced Thursday by the FBI and Justice Department, represents the latest law enforcement effort in recent years to go after a broad-based hacking campaign known to the private sector as Flax Typhoon.

The tools at issue, called “Microscan” and “FishHub,” were used by the hackers to scan, phish and hack targets that included U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure, officials said. Microscan was used to target, among other entities, an unnamed power company in the U.S., Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese universities, a multinational, nongovernmental organization and Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies. And “FishHub” facilitated phishing activity that gave hackers remote access to victim networks, the FBI said.

The latest operation has rendered the tools inoperable in what FBI and Justice Department officials said was a blow to the hacking operation.

“We aim to remove the capability from the threat actors. We target their infrastructure, their money, and their tools,” FBI Cyber Division Deputy Assistant Director Jason Bilnoski said in an interview with The Associated Press, calling the hacking operation “indiscriminate and reckless.”

The tools were operated by a Chinese-based information security company called Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI says has contracts with the Chinese government. The company is regarded by the FBI as the true identity of Flax Typhoon.

In Beijing, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China has always cracked down on hacking activities in accordance with the law. Mao said Beijing also firmly opposes spreading disinformation and creating confusion for political purposes, adding that maintaining cybersecurity is a shared concern of both countries.

“We urge the U.S. to abandon its double standards and political manipulation, and work with China through equal dialogue and consultation to jointly address cybersecurity risks,” she said.

In September 2024, the FBI announced that it had disrupted a massive botnet associated with Flax Typhoon that installed malicious software on more than 200,000 consumer devices, including cameras, video recorders and home and office routers, to create a massive botnet. The botnet, or network of infected computers, was used to facilitate cyber crimes, such as the theft of sensitive information from victims’ networks.

FBI San Diego Supervisory Special Agent Brett Lally said that the department would continue to monitor for ways that the company might rebuild its infrastructure.

“It’ll be interesting to see what this round of disruption actions have in terms of their ability to operate as a company in China,” Lally said.

—Safiyah Riddle and Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Microsoft and Adobe are suspended from H-1B visa program, with Vance accusing the tech giants of fraud
item.description:
Microsoft and Adobe have been suspended from the H-1B visa program, Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday, amid accusations that they and other companies have extensively abused the system to hire cheaper labor.

“This is a great day for American workers, because we are taking some very concrete actions to cut down on some of the H-1B and J-1 visa fraud that we’ve been tracking over the past several months,” Vance said at a Thursday morning press conference.

Microsoft and Adobe did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The J-1 visa is for foreign students, teachers, researchers and a few other visitor categories. The H-1B program allows companies to hire nonimmigrant foreign workers for roles that require specialized knowledge when they can’t be filled by the U.S. workforce.

Vance said the latter program has become “rife with fraud over the last several years—probably the last several decades.”

Rather than use H-1B visas for their intended purpose, he said, companies and outsourcing firms are using it to replace American workers “with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” who are “being mistreated by their employers and being used to undercut the wages of American workers.”

Broader Trump crackdown

The announcements follow an executive order in September that announced a review of the program’s application data, alleging “large-scale, systematic abuse” by companies.

The order—which comes from an administration whose attacks on science and research have been documented extensively—also characterized the abuse as a national security threat for discouraging Americans from “pursuing careers in science and technology.” 

The Trump administration has taken other actions to rein in H-1B visas, including last year’s announcement of a $100,000 fee for new applications, causing backlash and legal challenges.

Roughly 400,000 H-1B visas were approved in 2024, according to Pew Research, more than double the number approved in 2000.

Tech companies singled out

Vance said that no company has abused the program more than Microsoft, which he said laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from “6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.”

The secretary of Labor, Keith Sonderling, also announced that the program would no longer take applications from several major outsourcing firms, which supply companies with foreign candidates.

The U.S. tech industry relies heavily on H-1B workers, who earn on average 16% less than their American counterparts, according to a National Bureau of Economic Research paper.

In the 2024 fiscal year, 64% of H-1B visa recipients worked in computer-related occupations, according to federal data.

The H-1B program “is now the major pathway for employment-based immigrants to enter and stay in the United States,” according to a study published in International Migration Review this year, creating a power imbalance between employers and migrant workers.

Criticism across party lines

Criticism of the H-1B program has previously caused infighting among Trump’s associates, and crossed party lines.

Bernie Sanders said last year that he disagrees with claims by Elon Musk and other tech titans that the program is vital due to a scarcity of highly-skilled American workers.

The independent senator from Vermont said that corporations will lay off American workers while hiring new H-1B workers, even though U.S. Census data indicates that millions of Americans with advanced STEM degrees are not employed in their field.

“The cheaper the labor they hire, the more money the billionaires make,” Sanders said.

At the press conference, Vance said the government also sees “a lot of J-1 visa fraud,” naming nine universities “that we believe merit an investigation,” claiming they employ J-1 visa students to work on federally funded grants at a rate much higher than the national average.

“We cannot allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest to use them to undercut the wages of American workers,” Vance said.

“Now, it’s one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk,” he added. “Obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that.”

Musk, who immigrated from South Africa, has previously defended the H-1B program, vowing that “I will go to war on this issue.”

He has held both J-1 and H-1B visas, and has been accused of violating the terms of the former, which he has denied. His company, Tesla, is also facing a class action lawsuit that alleges it of having a “systematic preference” for hiring H-1B visa holders and disproportionately firing U.S. citizens.

Shares of Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT) fell after the announcement on Thursday, closing 1.35% lower. But the stock was up about 1% in premarket trading on Friday as of this writing.

Adobe Inc (Nasdaq: ADBE) stock was up 3.56% on Thursday despite the announcement.

item.title: The Trump administration just cut down a century’s worth of history at a D.C. golf course
item.description:
Workers removed more than 500 trees over the weekend at a Washington, D.C., golf course that President Donald Trump is working to remodel. It happened like many of his other design projects around town: suddenly and without permission.

Preservationists asked a judge Sunday to halt the Trump administration after it removed 529 trees Saturday at East Potomac Park, a golf course managed by the National Park Service, and on Monday, a judge called the removal “inexcusable.”

The course is home to elms, oaks, pines, and willows, as well as some of the 3,000 Japanese flowering cherry trees gifted by the government of Japan in 1912. Together they told the story of golf’s rise in America from a mostly treeless game on the U.S. coasts to a sport known for its big, lush vegetation. Now, just like that, a century’s worth of landscape design history has been torn up.

The removal happened “faster than anticipated,” according to the lawsuit, and the Trump administration didn’t meet its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, attorneys representing the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers said in a filing seeking an emergency action to pause further tree removal.

“‘Pulling a fast one’ has become the model this administration uses to circumvent the laws intended to protect the environment and D.C. landmarks,” Abbe D. Lowell, a founding member of Lowell & Associates, which is representing the plaintiffs along with Democracy Forward and Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “It did so with the East Wing and the Kennedy Center, and we are continuing our effort to stop them before they succeed in destroying D.C.’s historic public golf course.”

A brief history of parkland courses

East Potomac Park sits on a small island in the Potomac River, just south of the National Mall. Its earliest known vegetation consisted of tall grass and willow trees, most of which were cleared to design the first golf course in 1917. Over the years, more trees were added to adapt to changing tastes, according to a 2017 cultural landscape inventory of the course conducted by the Urban Heritage Project from the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design.

The first course at East Potomac Park was designed by golf course architect Walter J. Travis, who cleared the fairways of most willows but kept some existing trees along the course’s perimeter to separate the front and back nine. A new style of golf course design in the 1920s called parkland style, however, meant more trees would eventually be planted over the years.

As golf grew more popular and moved inland, parkland courses came to be known for their big, mature trees. The popularity of televised golf tournaments beginning in the 1950s and ’60s only made lush, green, gorgeous park-like backdrops that more appealing, according to the inventory, like the Masters Tournament in Augusta, Georgia, with its trees and plants imported from around the world in bloom.

At East Potomac Park, the Civilian Conservation Corps planted cedar trees in 1939 and additional trees in the 1960s and ’70s, including crab apple trees. The 2017 inventory also counted large wolf trees, large willow oaks, and a large American elm.

Some trees were planted for reasons of gameplay, not just aesthetics. The park’s miniature golf course, for example, was designed around a limited number of trees that function as hazards, and the park’s White Course has few trees and open fairways, making it popular with less competitive players.

The 2017 inventory noted that the park needed some care, including clearing invasive vines and trees that were were damaging some of the cherry trees. It also said that a “piecemeal nature of planting” had resulted in “a variety of mature trees and shrubs scattered throughout the landscape” that had no overall harmony.

A “surprise demolition”

But those suing Trump’s Interior Department and National Park Service say the administration’s tree razing went far above routine maintenance or a thoughtful pruning, and that the administration had even removed healthy, mature oaks and maple trees.

“Unleashing a surprise demolition razing over 500 historic trees in this public park and claiming it is part of maintenance from a dated, years-old landscaping plan is yet another brazen, lawless power grab that has become routine for the Trump administration,” Democracy Defenders Fund executive chair Norm Eisen said in a statement.

Trump’s planned makeover of the park (he had rubble from the White House’s East Wing demolition taken there) is part of a larger takeover of the federal government golf course system. Trump is reportedly offering his Trump International Golf Club West Palm Beach in Florida as an official U.S. government golf course for presidents that his family’s company would continue to operate.

Like the rings of a tree tell its story, the landscape design of East Potomac Park told a story of a game that grew up to appreciate the value of mature trees and ample vegetation as it became more popular. With the Trump administration’s sudden tree removal, part of that history is now gone.

item.title: Congress wants to keep AM radio in every new car
item.description:
In the era of streaming music and satellite radio, traditional broadcast stations are easy to overlook. AM radio, in particular, has fallen out of favor with younger drivers. So it’s perhaps no surprise that some automakers have begun dropping it from new vehicles. Congress, however, wants to put a stop to that.

Last month, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 979, the “AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act of 2025.” The bill is now on the Senate’s legislative calendar and has broad bipartisan support. The Senate also has a companion bill, S. 315, which cleared committee last year and is awaiting a floor vote.

While AM radio is dominated by political talk shows, religious programming, and sports, it still draws a sizable audience. The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), which supports the congressional effort, says more than 80 million Americans listen to AM each month.

The group describes AM radio as “a platform for locally produced content that is relevant to their audience and speaks to their unique cultural and linguistic needs.” It also notes that AM stations have historically provided an entry point into radio ownership for racial and ethnic minorities.

Automakers, meanwhile, are grappling with tariffs and rising component costs, and looking for ways to trim expenses. Removing AM radio wouldn’t shave hundreds or thousands of dollars off a vehicle’s price, but it could offer modest savings.

Electric vehicle makers face another challenge: The technology that powers EVs can interfere with AM radio reception.

“The high-voltage electrical systems in EVs generate electromagnetic interference that, according to the Center for Automotive Research, ‘distorts AM radio signals, affecting the listening experience for drivers and passengers.’ In other words: really staticky,” said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, in 2024 congressional testimony. “It’s not possible to eliminate that interference, and techniques to reduce interference add weight and mess with battery range and would cost an estimated $3.8 billion.”

Bozzella also argued that requiring AM radio amounted to a government mandate with no public safety justification.

Supporters of the legislation dispute that argument. AM stations play a significant role in the nation’s emergency alert infrastructure, including a FEMA-supported network of radio stations equipped to continue broadcasting during disasters.

Bozzella’s position was echoed by the then-president and CEO of the Consumer Technology Association, who wrote in a letter to the editor of The Washington Post that “a federal mandate that every car comes equipped with an AM radio in 2024 and beyond is like mandating that they come equipped with ashtrays or 8-track players.”

Still, traditional radio may have more life left in it than skeptics think, even as music streaming subscriptions approach 1 billion worldwide.

As more Americans return to the office, radio has benefited from renewed interest. Edison Research’s “Share of Ear” report, released in July, found that AM/FM radio accounted for 62% of ad-supported audio listening among adults, compared with just 6% for Spotify’s ad-supported service. In cars, AM/FM commanded an even larger share of ad-supported audio listening: 82% among adults 18 and older.

Whether the Senate will vote on the AM radio bill before November’s midterm elections remains unclear. And despite its bipartisan support, its prospects at the White House are uncertain.

The auto industry may oppose the measure, but it has some influential backers beyond the broadcasting industry, including the American Farm Bureau Federation, AARP, and a coalition of public safety organizations.

item.title: Elon Musk quietly becomes the biggest donor in the midterms in a bid to save Republicans
item.description:
Elon Musk, the world’s only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress.

The numbers, first reported by The New York Times ahead of this week’s federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk’s super PAC.

The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times.

Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024.

Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk’s efforts.

It’s a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough,” he said at the time.

Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared onstage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president’s second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency.

He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week.

Musk’s net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.

Republicans have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts—a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president’s performance, stubbornly high prices, and the unpopular war with Iran.

They have been using the money to blanket the airwaves in the race’s final stretch.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told the Times.

Democrats responded to the news by accusing Republicans of using vast amounts of cash to mask their shortcomings.

“Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president, and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

—By Jill Colvin, Associated Press

item.title: IMF boosts this year’s global economy growth outlook, but warns of risks from AI and debt
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including the financial frenzy around artificial intelligence.

The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1% pace this year. That’s up from its July forecast for 3.0% growth and well below the 3.5% expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4%, it said in its latest Economic Outlook.

The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gathered in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027.

Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1% this year, up from 2.0% in 2025, and then slow to 1.9% growth next year, it said.

The forecasts are based on a nearly 41% increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7% in 2026, falling to 4.1% next year. They are also based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate.

AI has uneven impacts

The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks.

Its benefits are not shared equally: The U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said.

“The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s director of research, told reporters in Bangkok.

Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95% of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April.

“The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says.

Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said.

Underscoring such concerns, sell-offs of AI-related shares swept through Asia on Tuesday, with South Korea’s Kospi sinking as much as 7% before it closed 5.5% lower.

AI’s effects on employment are another worry, “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.

“The impact over time on jobs globally we estimate to be around 40%—jobs either augmented or downgraded or eliminated. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said.

Debt remains a key concern for regional economies

The IMF chief is urging countries to do a better job of improving their national finances and taming mounting levels of debt.

That’s especially crucial at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said.

Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7% this year from 4.5% in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4% annual pace.

The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions’ economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3% rate of growth in 2027.

The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by a meager 1.1% this year and 1.2% in 2027.

China, the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5% this year, down from 5% in 2025, in line with the government’s official target.

India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7% clip, down from a sizzling 7.7% last year.

The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth.

—By Elaine Kurtenbach, AP business writer

Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed.

item.title: Getty Images was worth $4.8 billion just 4 years ago. Now it’s filing for bankruptcy

Getty Images is filing for bankruptcy and plans to go private, the company announced on Monday.A release says that the company plans to begin the process of filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the weeks ahead and undergo massive restructuring, which will ultimately see complete control and ownership of the company in the hands of the Getty family, as well as Koch Equity Development.

As a part of the restructuring, Koch Equity Development (which is the investment arm of Koch, Inc.) will invest up to $533 million, and as the process progresses, the company will “continue to operate in the normal course,” and “vendors will be unaffected and paid in full in the ordinary course of business,” according to the company’s release.

Getty is perhaps best known as a source of photographs and stock images used for a variety of purposes, and has faced significant headwinds with the advent of AI-generated imagery in recent years. Notably, in a recent investor presentation, company materials noted that there was “declining agency demand and disruption to the iStock eCommerce business. It had also announced plans to merge with Shutterstock in January—a plan that has since been scrapped.

Even so, company leadership says that it’s confident that going private and restructuring will help it regain its footing.

Mark Getty, Getty Images’ co-founder and chairman of the board, said in the company release that he was “pleased to continue our strong partnership with Koch Equity Development and the lender groups to provide capital structure improvements that will enable us to build on our solid foundation and seize new growth opportunities.”

Additionally, Mike Harris, senior managing director and co-head at Koch Equity Development, said that the group remains “confident in the company’s future and fully support this transaction alongside the Getty family. This equity investment will provide Getty Images with a firm financial foundation and greater flexibility to continue investing in its employees, customers, contributors, and future growth.”

item.title: Bumble stock soars as the embattled dating app strikes deal to go private. Here’s how it got here
item.description:
Bumble has spent the past few years trying everything from a new CEO to AI-powered matches. 

Now, the embattled dating app company is making another big move: going private.

Ithaca Holdings, a new firm run by former tech executives, is acquiring Bumble for $1.3 billion, the latter announced on Tuesday. Bumble’s board unanimously voted in favor of the deal, with founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd recusing herself from the decision. 

News of a potential deal was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Bumble’s shareholders will receive $6.05 for each share of Class A Common Stock. According to Bumble, this is about 138% higher than its Friday, October 9, closing share price and around 119% over its 30-day weighted average price ending Friday. 

The dating app company was valued at about $335 million at the end of business on Friday. 

Ithaca’s co-CEOs and co-founders, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will take over as co-CEOs of Bumble and “partner with Wolfe Herd to extend Bumble’s original vision to help people find connections in life and love into the next era.” 

For anyone wondering what this arrangement might look like, this line in the announcement provides a pretty good idea: “Ithaca’s mission is to apply frontier technology to renew and accelerate businesses that enrich people’s lives and create lasting value in a world transformed by AI.” 

Blackstone, which owns a stake in Bumble, has approved the deal.

Wolfe Herd sang Ithaca’s praises, stating, “In Ithaca, we have found a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future.”

Bumble’s journey as a public company

Bumble went public in February 2021, making founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd the youngest woman to take a company public or become a self-made billionaire. It was a success story. 

However, in the five-plus years since, the company has struggled to stay relevant in a world that has grown increasingly tired of dating apps. 

As of October 5, shares of Bumble Inc. (Nasdaq: BMBL) were down almost 95% from their opening high. The stock has had a relatively steady decline over its half a decade of trading. 

That all changed on Monday when news broke of a potential sale. While still over $80 lower than its record high, Bumble’s shares closed up 49.61%. As of publication, the stock has been fluctuating close to 4% up during premarket trading. 

Attempts to stay relevant in recent years

Dating apps of all shapes and sizes have faced a decline as Gen Z, in particular, moves away from online dating. Match Group-owned Hinge is a notable exception to the trend.

Wolfe Herd stepped down as CEO in January 2024, transitioning to the position of executive chair. Her successor, Lidiane Jones—a former Slack CEO—soon cut about 350 roles. 

Jones’s tenure didn’t last very long, with Wolfe Herd returning as CEO in March 2025.

A few months later, Bumble cut another 240 positions, about 30% of its workforce. Shortly after, Wolfe Herd threatened to remove “members with low-quality and incomplete profiles” in a focus on quality over quantity. 

Bumble has also paid attention to its non-romantic ventures. In November 2025, the company launched a new standalone BFF app.

Like many tech CEOs, Wolfe Herd has turned to AI as a potential draw for users. In May, Bumble launched an AI assistant called Bee. Bumble calls Bee a matchmaker, with the tool meant to replace the need to swipe. The company is also testing out having Bee create dates for matches. 

Then, in August, Bumble announced it would be getting rid of its distinguishing feature: women messaging first. 

The company cited a 2024 internal survey that found two-thirds of women felt less pressure around dating when men made the first move. At the time, the company launched its Opening Move feature, which allowed men to make the first move using preset prompts and gave women 24 hours to respond or the match expired. 

Now, anyone can message and users have 72 hours to respond. 

“Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides,” Wolfe Herd said in the announcement. “This evolution isn’t a departure from our founding vision, but the realization of it.”

item.title: Character.ai has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as it moves to sell assets to Disney
item.description:
Controversial chatbot platform Character.ai is seeking Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the wake of mounting legal challenges and runaway operating costs, the four-year-old startup said in a surprise announcement on Monday.

The move comes as the Menlo Park, California, company has faced a number of lawsuits in recent years, including some that say its AI companions have encouraged users to harm or kill themselves.

In its announcement, Character.ai said it has reached an agreement with Disney Worldwide Services, an affiliate of the Walt Disney Company, to sell some of its intellectual property for $20 million and “transition services” that will help Character.ai continue to operate, at least temporarily.

“Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” CEO Colin Adams said in a statement. “After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders.”

In a blog post, the company said its platform “remains up and running” as it seeks to figure out a path forward. It expects the sale process to be completed by November or early December.

item.title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
item.description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Bank of America stock falls in the wake of a historic $1.2 billion fine after it failed to report financial crime
item.description:
Bank of America has been fined over $1.2 billion for violating anti-money-laundering and sanction laws. 

On Tuesday, October 13, the U.S. Department of the Treasury handed down the fine, stating that Bank of America had failed to report over $5 billion in “suspicious activity” to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). 

Over $1 billion of the activity was “national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury stated in its announcement. 

“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risk,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Third largest in history

The $1.2 billion fine is the Treasury Department’s third largest in its history. In 2023, it fined Binance $3.4 billion and, a year later, fined TD Bank $1.3 billion. 

The total figure includes a $750 million fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)—the largest in its history—for having an “ineffective” anti-money laundering program. 

It also comprised an $11.6 million settlement agreement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). While this is the smallest part of the fine, the 475 “apparent violations of sanction programs” are quite notable. These sanctions were against Russia, Iran, global terrorism, and narcotics, among other significant areas. 

According to the Treasury, “these apparent violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error.”

“We are responsible for getting it right”

Reached for comment by Fast Company, a Bank of America spokesperson said the financial services giant has invested “billions of dollars” in financial crime and is committed to addressing the issues raised by U.S. regulators.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 OCC Consent Order and FinCEN’s investigation.”

Stock down after third-quarter earnings

Shares of Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC) were down more than 8% on Wednesday following the fine and an early-morning earnings report.

The company reported $30.12 billion in revenue for quarter three, falling short of Wall Street’s predicted $30.69 billion, according to consensus estimates cited by CNBC.

“Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share,” Bank of America’s statement said. “We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base.”

item.title: ‘No Kings’ October 17 protest: 2,500 rallies, marches, and parties in all 50 states urge Americans to vote early in midterm election
item.description:
The “No Kings” movement, which began as a populist protest against the Trump administration, has now morphed into a get-out-the-vote movement ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.

On Saturday, October 17, “No Kings: Vote Early” is scheduled to take place, and more than 2,500 events are on the map in all 50 states. Organizers are preparing a range of events, from protests to neighborhood block parties and cookouts, with a focus on ensuring free and fair elections in November.

Marches, rallies, and voter fairs related to early voting are scheduled for several major U.S. cities, including San Francisco, Atlanta, Washington, D.C., New York, and Los Angeles. There will also be events in Boston, Philadelphia, and Austin. (See a full list of events here.)

The day is being organized by a broad coalition of nonprofits, educators, unions, and progressive political groups. These include the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), American Federation of Teachers, Black Voters Matter Fund, 50501, Indivisible, League of Women Voters, MoveOn, Public Citizen, State Voices, and Voto Latino. (A full list of partners is available here.)

“Early and record turnout is our best chance to ensure every vote is counted and election results are too big to rig,” Joel Payne, chief communications officer for MoveOn Civic Action, tells Fast Company.

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, No Kings protests have drawn millions of people in large cities and small towns across America. The last protest, on March 28, was attended by an estimated 9 million people.

Now organizers are taking that message to the ballot box. Unlike previous protests, the coming event will include walks to polling stations, voter planning drives, and local election defense workshops.

“In order to protect our voting rights, the ACLU has identified dozens of scenarios for election interference and voter disenfranchisement across the country and prepared to respond immediately with legal action and community mobilization,” Deirdre Schifeling, the organization’s chief political and advocacy officer, tells Fast Company. “Together with our affiliates and partners, we have built a powerful network of organizers, community leaders, and tens of thousands of volunteers who are ready to navigate attacks on our elections and assist voters.”

“No one gets to scare us out of our vote, and on October 17th, we’re showing up, fiercely and fearlessly, to show the power of the American vote,” adds Beatriz Lopez, executive director of Voto Latino.

item.title: Florida can now enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids
item.description:
The state of Florida won a key court decision Wednesday that allows it to enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids under 14 and other restrictions.

The law was one of the most restrictive in the U.S. on social media use by children when Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it in 2024.

The law implicates the First Amendment, an appeals court said, but “likely does so in a content-neutral manner.”

It would likely survive a full legal challenge “because it doesn’t burden substantially more speech than necessary to advance the important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction,” a panel from the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 3-0 opinion.

The law bans social media accounts for Florida children under 14 and requires parental consent for use by kids who are 14 or 15.

Industry trade groups the Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice sued Florida, arguing that the law violated the free-speech rights of social media providers and users. A judge in 2025 said the law likely was unconstitutional and granted an injunction.

That injunction was put on hold while the appeals court heard the case. The lawsuit, with the injunction now overturned, will return to federal court in Tallahassee.

The appeals court noted that the law covers social media platforms “that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.”

An email seeking comment from the Florida attorney general’s office was not immediately answered. NetChoice said it was disappointed with the decision.

“We are currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families,” said Paul Taske, a lawyer at NetChoice.
